Mica. A group of silicate minerals characterised by perfect basal cleavage, which means they split easily into thin, flexible sheets. The two most common varieties are muscovite, a potassium-aluminium mica, and biotite, an iron-magnesium mica. They're common in granites, schists, and other metamorphic rocks, and their sheet structure gives them unique optical and thermal properties.

Micas are silicate minerals with a layered crystal structure. The atoms are arranged in sheets bonded by weak forces perpendicular to the layers. This perfect basal cleavage is a hallmark feature for field identification—the sheets split easily into thin, transparent or translucent layers. Muscovite is colourless to pale, while biotite is dark brown to black. Both are common in granites.

Micas are rated two point five to three on the Mohs hardness scale, relatively soft, though their hardness varies depending on the direction you scratch them. They're thermally insulating and electrically insulating in the basal direction. Historically, they've been used in electrical insulation and as a window pane substitute. Mica weathers slowly because the sheet structure resists chemical attack, so mica flakes persist in sediments longer than feldspar or other minerals.

Mica is a primary constituent of granite, appearing alongside feldspar and quartz. It's a companion mineral in granites and metamorphic rocks. Mica is abundant in schist, gneiss, and other high-grade metamorphic rocks. It's at the soft end of the hardness scale, easily scratched by feldspar and quartz, yet its unique structure makes it one of the most distinctive minerals to identify in the field.
